events.title: The death of St. Benedict of Nursia
events.shortBlurb: The father of Western monasticism, whose Rule ordered the prayer and work of countless monasteries, died at Monte Cassino…
body: Born about 480 at Nursia, of a noble family and the twin brother of Scholastica, Benedict fled the corruption of the Roman schools, living three years as a hermit in a cave above Subiaco, secretly served by the monk Romanus.

Disciples gathered, and after ruling twelve small monasteries he went up, about 529, to Monte Cassino, overthrew a shrine of Apollo, and founded his abbey. There he wrote his Rule, 'a school of the Lord's service', whose life of prayer, reading, and labor under an abbot won the whole West.

All we surely know of his end comes from the second book of Gregory the Great's Dialogues. Six days before it he ordered his grave opened; then, as fever took him, he was carried into the oratory, received the Body and Blood of Christ, and died standing, upheld between his disciples, his hands lifted to heaven.

It was 21 March, in a year tradition reckons as 547; he was laid beside Scholastica, whose soul he had seen ascend as a dove three days after her death. Father of Western monasticism, he was proclaimed a patron of Europe by Paul VI in 1964, and his feast is kept on 11 July.

events.title: The founding of Cîteaux
events.shortBlurb: St. Robert of Molesme and his companions withdrew to a Burgundian wilderness to keep the Rule of St. Benedict in its purity, founding the Cistercian order…
body: On 21 March 1098, the feast of St Benedict, which that year fell on Palm Sunday, Robert, abbot of Molesme, led twenty-one companions out of his Burgundian abbey to a marsh in the diocese of Châlons, ceded to them by Raynald, viscount of Beaune. Among its rushes — cistels in the local speech — they raised the New Monastery, to keep the Rule of St Benedict to the letter.

Authorized by the papal legate Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, the venture survived its founder: within a year Robert was ordered back to Molesme, and the prior Alberic took his place, clothing the monks in their white habit, instituting lay brothers, and winning the protection of the Holy See in 1100. From Cîteaux, in Latin Cistercium, the new observance took its name.

Under Alberic's successor, the Englishman Stephen Harding, Bernard entered in 1112 with thirty companions, and colonies went out to La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond. Stephen's Charter of Charity bound the houses into one order under a yearly general chapter; at his death in 1134 it counted seventy monasteries, and by 1152 some three hundred and fifty.
